extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of English literature and theater history (including editors of Shakespearean texts)
extracted.subtask_description: A focused account of Elizabethan stage practice (theaters, stages, companies, presentation) and the textual transmission/publication of plays in Shakespeare's era, aimed at informing interpretation, editing, and historical staging decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic and tragic tendencies (1616–1642)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedies from 1616 to 1642 reveal two chief influences: realistic and satiric, following Jonson, or light-hearted, lively combinations of manners and intrigue, after Fletcher; tragi-comedies follow Fletcher with authorial variations; tragedies usually mingle lust, devilish intrigue, physical horror (after Webster and Tourneur) often with romantic variation and a technic of suspense and surprise similar to Beaumont and Fletcher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these genre distinctions to classify plays of the period and to understand their tone, plot devices, and character types; the same author may write in different modes (e.g., Massinger, Shirley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastoral play and court masque characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastoral drama attempted a full dramatic exposition of the golden age (in imitation of Guarini) but never won popular hold; the masque developed at court into an elaborate entertainment centered on masked dance plus dialogue, spectacle, music, grotesque dances, and elaborate setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect pastoral elements scattered across plays rather than sustained dramatic practice; masques relied on architecture and court resources (e.g., Inigo Jones) and therefore differ sharply from public-theatre practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public theater architecture and layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Public theaters were usually round or nearly round wooden buildings of three stories with tiers of galleries encircling an open-air pit; the stage projected into the pit, had dressing rooms in the rear, a 'hut' above for machinery, and sometimes pillars supporting a roof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These architectural features shaped audience proximity, acoustics, entrance/exit distances, and visual focus—factors crucial for reconstructing staging, blocking, and audience interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Companies of actors: cooperative, licensed, and patronized
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies were cooperative organizations of eight or ten actors who leased theaters, hired supernumeraries, bought plays, and shared profits; in Elizabeth's reign they obtained licenses from noble patrons and later came under royal patronage (e.g., King's men).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The business organization informs authorship, ownership of play texts, mobility of plays (touring), and why actors or companies might control publication decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage presentation: no scenery, no women actors, front-stage action
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional presentations lacked scenery and women actors (female parts were taken by boys); most action occurred on the projecting front stage (open on three sides) rather than behind curtains, and scenes often give no precise locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect plays of the period to be written for a bare front stage; directors and editors should avoid assuming modern scenic specificity when interpreting stage directions or textual locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of front-stage configuration for playwrighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because there was no drop-curtain and the front stage projected into the audience, play texts were composed with entrances/exits across distance, scenes that often lack precise locality, and frequent use of processions (tragedy ends with funeral procession) or dances (comedy ends with a dance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing structure or pace, account for the need to clear the stage at scene/end and for theatrical conventions (procession or dance) embedded in plot resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner stage functions (four summarized uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Specific, restricted, and usually propertied locality (cave, study, shop, prison); 2) Scenes requiring discovery or tableaux (curtains drawn to present a set piece); 3) Propertied backgrounds (forest, church, temple) used as scenic background; 4) Indicating change of scene—opening curtains reveals a special background and marks a distinct place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four functions explain the inner stage's role in signaling locality, enabling discoveries/tableaux, and effecting rapid scene changes without modern scenery; editors and directors should interpret references to curtains, galleries, and inner-stage properties accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gallery, doors, and windows as scenic shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: The gallery could represent a wall, an upper story, or an elevated locality; doors represented house doors or city gates; windows or balconies served as houses' windows—these elements provided specific locality cues without elaborate scenery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage directions mentioning galleries/doors/windows are pragmatic cues for spatial relations and sightlines rather than detailed scenic prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of properties and costume in spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Although lacking scenery, Elizabethan performance employed processions, battles, mythological beings, ascents/descents, fireworks, and elaborate properties; costumes were often lavish and anachronistic though sometimes attention was paid to appropriateness (e.g., shepherds in white).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle relied on properties and costume more than scenery; budgeting and casting choices historically prioritized costume and processionary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance duration and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of a play seems usually to have been completed in two hours; there was sometimes music between the acts, but no long waits and little stage business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect concise scenes and brisk pacing in original performances; modern productions can consider historical timing when editing or staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution from medieval platea to modern picture-frame stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The front stage functioned as the medieval platea; inner and upper stages as localized domus/loca; with the Restoration and use of scenery the inner stage and proscenium grew in importance until the modern picture-frame stage evolved from the Elizabethan inner stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding this evolution clarifies why Elizabethan plays mix neutral and localized spaces and why later scenic practices altered interpretation and staging conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual transmission difficulty: absence of manuscripts and authorial supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Main difficulties for determining Shakespeare's texts are the total absence of manuscripts and the fact that dramatists regarded plays as material for performance (not for print), often permitting plays to be printed without supervision or apparently without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must therefore weigh multiple imperfect sources (Quartos, Folios, playhouse copies) and be alert to corruption from performance transcription or actor memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pirated (reported) Quartos: identifying signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain Quartos (e.g., first quartos of Romeo and Juliet, Henry V, Merry Wives, Hamlet, Pericles) show 'clear traces' of surreptitious reporting: corrupt and mangled text, errors from 'copied only by the ear', slips of memory, and variants attributable to mistakes of the ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Quartos showing those features as 'reported' and assess them critically; where a later Quarto or Folio is available, compare to detect restorations or corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher/Stationers' Register practices and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers entered works on the Stationers' Register to establish monopoly against piracy, but the Company protected members more than authors; entry could be withheld until authority was shown and pirated texts were sometimes published or later authentic editions still issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/practical registration does not guarantee textual authenticity; bibliographical evidence (register entries, dates, transfers) must be combined with textual analysis to establish provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining prime authority for a play text (Quarto vs Folio)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases a Quarto (usually the most recent) provided the text used in the First Folio; in some plays the extant Quarto rather than the Folio is the prime authority today; the Folio sometimes represents an independent source, and in a few cases reported texts form the only authority (e.g., Pericles in the third Folio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions should assess whether the Folio or a particular Quarto represents the more authoritative text by examining registration history, textual variants, and internal evidence of performance-based corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial and actor attitudes toward printing plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary authors (e.g., Heywood, Marston) often considered printing plays undesirable or dishonest—selling to the stage was seen as relinquishing rights; some plays were published 'without his consent' and thus appeared in corrupt forms; some actors thought printing was against their pecuniary interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These attitudes explain why authorized texts are uneven and why some authors later sought to produce corrected editions; historical context of publication motives should inform textual editorial practice.
